Abstract This study aims to examine how management control systems (MCS), particularly those enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI), shape the implementation of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) strategies and influence the overall performance of financial institutions in Morocco. Drawing on an integrated conceptual framework that synthesizes Simons’ (1995) levers of control—comprising belief systems, boundary systems, diagnostic control systems, and interactive control systems—with Reynaud’s (2003) holistic model of overall performance, which emphasizes the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of organizational performance, the study investigates how these complementary perspectives jointly explain the embedding of CSR initiatives and their impact on overall performance. Empirical data were collected via a structured questionnaire administered to 45 executives and CSR managers from Moroccan financial institutions. The analysis was conducted using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that belief systems (β = 0.41, p < 0.01) and boundary systems (β = 0.36, p < 0.05) positively and significantly influence the implementation of CSR strategies by reinforcing organizational values and ethical standards. Diagnostic control systems (β = 0.29, p < 0.05), especially when enhanced by AI tools such as real-time monitoring and predictive analytics, contribute to improving CSR implementation and ensuring accurate and transparent ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) reporting. However, the study finds that interactive control systems do not have a statistically significant effect on CSR strategy nor on overall performance. Furthermore, CSR strategies act as a mediating variable between MCS and institutional performance (indirect effect β = 0.27, p < 0.05), emphasizing their strategic role in creating long-term value. These findings underscore the critical role of targeted control mechanisms and the integration of AI within management control frameworks to foster responsible business practices and drive multidimensional sustainability performance in the Moroccan financial sector performance. Introduction Organizations have increasingly recognized the importance of their engagement in social responsibility (CSR), which is no longer perceived as a mere managerial trend but as a fundamental strategic necessity. Over the years, CSR has evolved significantly, transitioning from philanthropic efforts to structured, regulated approaches that are now deeply embedded in organizational management practices. This transformation is largely driven by legislative frameworks governing CSR and by technological advancements, both of which serve as key drivers of innovation and sustainable development (Wirba, 2024). Indeed, societal considerations have become an essential strategic pillar for companies aiming to strengthen their competitive advantage in a constantly evolving and globalized economic environment (Kramer & Porter, 2011). Today, the integration of social, environmental, and ethical concerns into corporate strategies is no longer a discretionary initiative but a strategic imperative, aligning with the growing expectations of stakeholders (Lisi et al., 2023). Furthermore, socially responsible investors actively seek companies that embed CSR into their strategic framework, viewing them as lower risk and more attractive in the long term. This is particularly evident when firms leverage artificial intelligence to enhance their societal impact and improve CSR practices (Reda et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2023; Gallardo-Vázquez & Lizcano-Álvarez, 2020). Moroccan financial institutions are progressively integrating CSR into their operations. However, the structured implementation of CSR strategies, supported by effective management control systems, remains underdeveloped. While prior research has examined the motivations behind CSR adoption and its financial impact, few studies have explored the role of control systems in facilitating CSR and assessing its economic, social, and environmental effects within the Moroccan context (El Mouatassim & Youssef, 2023). This study utilizes Simons (1995) Levers of Control (LoC) framework, emphasizing the integration of management control systems with strategic goals. Moreover, artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative potential for enhancing management control systems and bolstering CSR performance (Mantouzi & Said, 2026). With AI-driven predictive analytics and machine learning, real-time data processing can significantly improve decision-making, risk management, transparency, and sustainability outcomes (Nweje & Taiwo, 2025; Ahmed et al., 2024). The integration of AI within CSR strategies introduces an innovative approach to promote sustainable business practices. As a strategic enabler, AI enhances regulatory compliance, deepens stakeholder engagement, and improves environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance (Nozari, 2024; Larbi-Siaw et al., 2022). Thus, investigating how AI can be incorporated into management control systems to support ESG governance and further corporate sustainability is essential. AI also facilitates real-time monitoring of both financial and nonfinancial performance, aligning corporate strategies with ESG indicators and sustainability objectives via advanced data collection, processing, and analysis (Rashid et al., 2025; Bhandari et al., 2025). The incorporation of technological advancements in CSR management not only meets the growing demands for social responsibility but also enhances overall performance, striking a balance between economic success, social impact, and environmental sustainability (Alketbi & Ahmad, 2024; Sigurdsson, 2024; Shiri & Jafari-Sadeghi, 2023; Mio et al., 2022; Ouriniche et al., 2022). This study builds upon Simons (1995) LoC framework, enriched by AI insights, to examine the role of management control mechanisms in implementing CSR strategies and their impact on the overall performance of Moroccan financial institutions. Additionally, we integrate Reynaud’s (2003) holistic performance model into our framework to offer a comprehensive view of global performance. On the basis of the literature, we formulate several hypotheses to explore the integration of AI in control systems, assess its influence on CSR execution, and analyze its contribution to corporate sustainability. This study first examines the role of belief systems, augmented by AI, in shaping CSR strategies and their impact on overall corporate performance (H1). Next, it investigates the influence of boundary systems, incorporating AI tools, in structuring CSR strategies and assessing their effect on corporate performance (H2). Additionally, the study analyzes the contribution of diagnostic control systems, optimized through AI, in operationalizing CSR strategies, highlighting the mediating role of CSR in enhancing corporate performance (H3). The role of interactive control systems, empowered by AI, in implementing CSR strategies and influencing overall performance is also explored (H4). Finally, the study evaluates the mediating role of CSR strategies in the relationship between AI-supported control levers and the corporate performance of financial institutions (H5). To empirically test these hypotheses, we employ partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4 (Hair et al., 2017). This research makes a significant contribution to the social and environmental management control literature, which has focused on external CSR disclosures at the expense of internal management processes. Furthermore, the study advances existing research by conceptually integrating Simons Levers of Control Framework (1995, 2000) with Reynaud’s holistic performance model (2003), offering a novel and integrated perspective on the interplay between MCSs and sustainable development. While research on CSR and management control systems has expanded in recent years, this study provides new empirical insights within the context of an emerging economy—Morocco. It particularly sheds light on the evolving landscape of Moroccan financial institutions, which are strengthening their presence in Africa and expanding into international markets. Our article is structured as follows: The first section is dedicated to a literature review, which serves as the foundation for formulating our research hypotheses. The second section presents the methodological tools used to conduct the empirical study. The third and fourth sections present the empirical results, discussion, and conclusions drawn from this research, respectively. 2. Review of the Literature and Research Hypotheses Corporate social responsibility has evolved significantly in recent decades, facilitated by the emergence of new standards and guidelines that encourage the adoption of responsible practices within organizations. However, integrating a CSR strategy requires the establishment of effective planning and control systems (Epstein, 2006; Perrini & Tencati, 2006; Gond et al., 2012). According to Kaplan & Norton (1996), for a strategy to be considered as such, it must be accompanied by performance measurement systems. Simons (1995) developed a theoretical framework highlighting the close relationship between strategy and control. He defines management control systems as "formalized procedures based on information that managers use to maintain or modify certain configurations of the company's activities". Simons framework is structured around four interrelated control levers—belief systems, boundary systems, diagnostic controls, and interactive controls—each playing a distinct yet complementary role in aligning organizational goals with strategic innovation. With the rise of new strategies, such as CSR, these four control levers are simultaneously activated for their framing, implementation, and evaluation. The author differentiates between various levers, considering diagnostic control systems and boundary systems as systems that guide employee behaviors through the implementation of rules and procedures aimed at achieving organizational objectives. In contrast, interactive control systems and belief systems promote core values, stimulate debate, encourage the search for strategic opportunities, and foster creative innovation (Simons, 1995; Arjaliès & Mundy, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mouatassim et al. (2026) 3 2013). Thus, control levers are designed to create both positive and negative forces, generating dynamic tension in the implementation of a CSR strategy (Henri, 2006; Widener, 2007; Kruis et al., 2016). Previous studies have demonstrated that this dialectical relationship between different control systems positively influences organizational performance (Asiaei et al., 2023; Fukaya, 2024; Bedford, 2015). The relationship between CSR strategy and control systems has given rise to the concept of overall performance, which is regarded in the academic literature as the implementation and evaluation of sustainable development strategies (Elkington, 1997; Capron & Quairel, 2006). The concept of overall performance is distinguished by its multidimensional nature and its ambition to provide an integrated view of various performance aspects. It goes beyond traditional evaluations that focus solely on economic and financial dimensions to include social and environmental aspects within a systemic approach (Reynaud, 2003). This integration relies on a coherent interaction between the different dimensions, structured around causal models that connect factors from heterogeneous fields (Chauvey & Naro, 2013; Capron & Quairel, 2006). Therefore, overall performance is not limited to a mere aggregation of economic, social, and environmental dimensions but is based on a holistic approach aimed at balancing and aligning these strategic issues (Reynaud, 2003; Baret, 2006; Jusoh et al., 2021). This alignment capability becomes even more crucial in a rapidly changing economic environment, where decision- making relies on increasingly complex data volumes. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) and business intelligence (BI) technologies serve as strategic levers to enhance corporate sustainability management. These technologies facilitate the real- time processing of financial, environmental, and social data, enabling continuous optimization of overall performance (Segun- Ajao, 2025; Rane et al., 2024; Ouriniche et al., 2022; Wamba-Taguimdje et al., 2020). 2.1. The role of AI-powered belief systems in guiding CSR strategy and managing overall performance. These belief systems within organizations are structured around a formal set of guiding principles, such as mission statements, goal definitions, and ethical charte rs; managers utilize these frameworks to communicate and reinforce the organization’s fundamental values and strategic objectives (Simons, 2000; Widener, 2007; Henri, 2006). While leadership primarily drives the communication of these values, it is essential that this effort is complemented by the active engagement of employees. Indeed, employee participation in CSR initiatives is pivotal for the successful execution of sustainable business strategies (Bauman & Skitka, 2012). The extant literature consistently demonstrates that every employee, whether directly or indirectly, influences the organization’s overall performance, thereby contributing to its reputation and long-term growth (Bernstein, 2018; Aguinis & Glavas, 2012). As organizational control mechanisms, belief systems aim to define, promote, and embed the fundamental values of an organization. They provide a structuring framework that enables managers to mobilize organizational resources to design high- performing strategies and enhance overall performance (Marginson et al., 2014; Asiaei et al., 2021). In the context of strategic transformation, these systems facilitate the integration of responsible values and guide stakeholders toward sustainability goals (Arjaliès & Mundy, 2013). Moreover, they play a key role in implementing sustainable development strategies while ensuring the preservation of the organization's identity and core principles (Jusoh et al., 2021). With the introduction of AI, a new dynamic has been infused into organizational belief systems. By enabling a more precise alignment of stakeholder behaviors with the company's strategic objectives, AI helps reinforce the coherence and scope of organizational principles (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018; Aghion et al., 2017). However, AI should be programmed to align with the organization's fundamental values. This integration occurs from the initial phase of the algorithmic decision-making process, when leaders define the goals of AI and balance the different interests within the organization (Zhao & Gómez Fariñas, 2023). In this context, AI also contributes to the strategic management of human resources by facilitating the identification of key competencies and ensuring better alignment between organizational values and strategic directions. By integrating advanced analytical tools, AI optimizes recruitment, training, and talent management, ensuring more effective convergence between corporate culture and internal dynamics (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2020). Thus, the integration of AI into organizational belief systems opens new perspectives in strategic management. It strengthens the coherence between a company’s core values and its performance and sustainability goals while adapting to the dynamics of an ever-evolving environment. We formulate the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 1: AI-powered belief systems support the framework of CSR strategy, which positively impacts overall performance. 2.2. The role of ai-driven boundary systems in framing CSR strategies and managing overall performance Boundary systems serve as critical control mechanisms that enable organizations to delineate acceptable behaviors by establishing rules, procedures, and codes of conduct. These systems are designed to mitigate risks and ensure alignment with strategic objectives (Arjaliès & Mundy, 2013; Simons, 1995). Their primary function is to regulate and monitor organizational activities, preventing deviations that could negatively impact corporate performance and reputation (Marginson et al., 2014). By defining precise operational limits, boundary systems help enforce regulatory compliance while proactively identifying errors and inefficiencies that may undermine internal processes and competitiveness (Fitri et al., 2024). https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mouatassim et al. (2026) 4 Among these mechanisms, codes of conduct play an essential role in guiding employees’ decision-making and strategic initiatives while maintaining alignment with responsible governance principles. These ethical standards are particularly crucial in CSR strategies, as they reinforce a sustainability-oriented corporate culture and ethical integrity (Collins, 2009). The integration of AI is transforming boundary systems by automating compliance processes, enhancing ethical awareness, and enabling real-time monitoring of organizational behavior. Recent research highlights AI’s contribution to strengthening adherence to ethical norms by automating employee training and increasing awareness of organizational conduct policies (Floridi et al., 2021). Furthermore, AI minimizes human biases in compliance enforcement, providing more objective and systematic monitoring of internal policies (Binns, 2018). AI-driven tools also enhance the anticipation and prevention of potential CSR violations by analyzing workforce behaviors to detect risk-prone activities or unsafe conditions, thereby enabling timely interventions (Kostynets & Kostynets, 2023). This proactive approach reduces workplace incidents and fosters a stronger culture of safety. Additionally, AI-powered technologies improve the reliability and impartiality of compliance processes by identifying issues such as discrimination, fraud, or conflicts of interest, thereby reinforcing transparency and organizational ethics (Zhao & Gómez Fariñas, 2023). This advanced analytical capacity further supports the early detection of noncompliance risks, allowing corrective measures to be taken before they compromise corporate social responsibility commitments (Dwivedi et al., 2023; Tambe et al., 2019). Moreover, AI plays a pivotal role in forecasting regulatory and societal changes, thereby enhancing corporate compliance with international standards and strengthening legitimacy among stakeholders (Baryannis et al., 2019). As organizations face increasing pressure to align with stakeholder expectations, AI-driven boundary systems provide a strategic advantage by ensuring responsible governance and adherence to evolving social imperatives (Sahed-Granger & Boncori, 2014; Perrini et al., 2011; Ferreira & Otley, 2009). The literature review underscores the critical role of intelligent boundary systems in structuring and executing CSR strategies. These systems facilitate the alignment of corporate practices with stakeholder expectations, anticipate compliance risks, and reinforce governance by ensuring a more rigorous and proactive application of ethical and regulatory standards. On the basis of these insights, we propose the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 2: AI-driven boundary systems facilitate the governance of CSR strategies, thereby exerting a positive effect on overall performance. 2.3. The role of diagnostic control systems in CSR strategy implementation and overall performance management Diagnostic control systems serve as essential feedback mechanisms that enable organizations to identify critical deviations from predefined performance standards (Simons, 1995; Abernethy & Brownell, 1999). These systems, which are traditionally employed by managers, facilitate the assessment and identification of key determinants for performance optimization (Fitri et al., 2024). The advent of AI has introduced transformative opportunities in leveraging these systems, providing innovative solutions to enhance the efficiency and impact of sustainability strategies (Sestino & De Mauro, 2022; Toniolo et al., 2020; Isensee et al., 2021). Through machine learning and natural language processing, AI enhances the extraction and analysis of relevant environmental, social, and governance (ESG) indicators, enabling more precise and comprehensive sustainability performance assessments (Bharadiya, 2023; Solaimani, 2024). By leveraging big data analytics, AI facilitates real-time ESG performance measurement, streamlining the collection, processing, and visualization of key performance indicators (KPIs), such as greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and supplier compliance with ethical standards (Burcă et al., 2024). In this context, the development of AI-driven sustainability indices and analytical dashboards—such as those powered by power BI— represents a significant advancement, simplifying the interpretation of complex datasets and providing decision-makers with actionable insights (Zhao & Gómez Fariñas, 2023). AI also plays a pivotal role in ESG reporting, offering a strategic tool with far-reaching implications. Its integration spans from data collection and management to report generation, verification, and utilization as a lever for sustainable performance (Paschen et al., 2020). In this context, De Villiers et al. (2024) propose a conceptual framework outlining four critical phases of AI-enhanced extrafinancial reporting: information management, report generation, data assurance, and report utilization. Their findings suggest that AI enables firms to optimize data governance, automate reporting processes, and enhance transparency while fostering more effective stakeholder engagement. These technological advancements significantly improve the accuracy, credibility, and accessibility of CSR reporting while simultaneously reducing associated costs and time constraints. Given these developments, AI-powered diagnostic control systems emerge as essential enablers of CSR strategies, ensuring that they remain a strategic priority rather than being overshadowed by purely commercial objectives (Gond et al., 2012). By integrating AI into performance management frameworks, organizations can drive responsible governance, strengthen compliance mechanisms, and enhance overall corporate sustainability. The role of interactive control systems in implementing CSR strategies and driving overall performance management Interactive control systems are formal mechanisms that enable organizational leaders to engage consistently in the decision-making processes of their subordinates (Simons, 2000). These systems are instrumental in discovering new ideas and promoting creativity while also clarifying strategic priorities for employees (Fitri et al., 2024; Semenova, 2021; Miles et al., 2006). However, their success hinges on leaders' ability to collaboratively formulate strategies with operational teams under conditions of uncertainty (Adi & Sukmawati, 2020). The effectiveness of these systems is also contingent upon the cognitive capabilities of decision-makers to assimilate and process the information exchanged during meetings, which ultimately enables the implementation of appropriate performance measurement systems and the adjustment of deviations identified through diagnostic control (Bonneveux & Saulquin, 2009; Simons, 2000). In this framework, interactive levers, supported by predictive algorithms and collaborative platforms, are pivotal in fostering organizational learning and innovation. These tools facilitate the optimization of strategic data analysis and interpretation, thereby strengthening the decision-making capacities of managers. Among the emerging tools, AI-based chatbots have proven especially useful in assisting leaders with CSR-related challenges. These intelligent assistants enable quick access to data from ESG reports, facilitating decision-making and significantly reducing the time spent on data analysis (Paschen et al., 2020). Furthermore, AI enhances nonfinancial reporting by streamlining processes while simultaneously improving the transparency and quality of decisions related to sustainability (Boloș et al., 2024). Its integration into predictive analytics, anomaly detection, and automated decision-making significantly improves the anticipation abilities of managers, allowing for more precise assessments of CSR performance and the adoption of well-informed strategies on the basis of a comprehensive analysis of data and a deeper understanding of emerging trends (Ravichandran, 2022). AI also plays a crucial role in the proactive management of risks and opportunities by leveraging interactive digital tools that enable the efficient analysis and dissemination of strategic information. This improves communication with stakeholders, ensuring enhanced transparency and the reliability of shared information, which in turn strengthens the credibility and efficacy of CSR initiatives (Reda et al., 2024; Bharadiya, 2023). Thus, AI is not limited to resource rationalization but serves as a strategic lever promoting proactive and sustainable management of environmental, social, and governance challenges. By integrating with interactive control systems, AI strengthens organizational learning and adaptability by facilitating real-time data analysis, risk anticipation, and the continuous improvement of CSR practices. These interactive systems, combined with the predictive and analytical capacities of AI, allow organizations to better meet sustainability requirements and optimize their communication with stakeholders. On the basis of these insights, we propose the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 4: AI-enhanced interactive control systems facilitate the implementation of CSR strategies, leading to a positive impact on overall performance. 2.5. Role of CSR strategy in managing overall performance In academic discourse, the evaluation of overall performance remains relatively underexplored, although the literature largely associates it with the effective implementation of CSR strategies (Capron & Quairel, 2006). Gond & Herrbach, (2006) conceptualize overall performance as an organization’s capacity to create value for its stakeholders by integrating economic, social, and environmental dimensions into its operational framework. Elkington’s seminal work in 1994 attempted to operationalize overall performance through the "Triple Bottom Line" framework. However, Elkington himself critiqued this model, arguing that it merely extends traditional economic and financial performance by incorporating a societal aspect, which could generate conflicts among the different performance dimensions (Elkington, 1999). In contrast, Reynaud (2003) proposes a more comprehensive approach by decomposing overall performance into three interconnected dimensions—economic, social, and environmental adopting an integrative and holistic perspective. Within this context, AI has emerged as a transformative tool for enhancing organizational performance in the ESG (environmental, social, and governance) domain, particularly as firms recognize the necessity of conducting business in a responsible and sustainable manner. AI not only optimizes data management and impact evaluation but also aids in the strategic alignment of CSR policies and practices with an organization’s long-term vision. Furthermore, AI facilitates the automation of ESG investment planning processes and various related tasks, such as stakeholder identification, variable assessment, and performance measurement, in line with predefined objectives (Zhao & Gómez Fariñas, 2023). Building upon Reynaud’s (2003) model, this study investigates the dimensions of overall performance and posits that the strategic use of Simons control systems, in conjunction with AI-powered tools, plays a critical role in shaping and operationalizing CSR strategies, ultimately driving improvements in overall performance. The integration of AI within these control systems ensures a more effective and proactive implementation of CSR, thereby enhancing the sustainability and performance outcomes of organizations (Figure 1). Building on these findings, we present the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 5: The implementation of a CSR strategy through AI-powered control levers positively impacts overall performance. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mouatassim et al. Adopted Research Methodology In this section, we provide a detailed overview of the structure of the survey, the characteristics of the participants, and the tools and measures used in the study. 3.1. Survey structure and participants To empirically test the research hypotheses derived from the literature review, we conducted a survey targeting all financial institutions in Morocco (Law 103-12 on Credit Institutions and Similar Entities). This decision was based on the relatively small size of the target population, which is composed of 90 institutions. For the empirical analysis, a hypothetico- deductive methodology was employed, using a structured questionnaire administered to key stakeholders, including senior executives, CSR managers, and management controllers. The questionnaire included Likert scale items to measure perceptions and attitudes toward CSR practices. Prior to the distribution of the questionnaire, a comprehensive documentary review was conducted to catalog the CSR practices implemented by these institutions. This review was based on publicly accessible materials, such as CSR charters and ESG reports, which were sourced from the official websites of the institutions. The questionnaire subsequently underwent a pretest involving three academic researchers and a statistician, all of whom affirmed the instrument's clarity and appropriateness. The survey was administered in two distinct phases. Initially, a list of relevant participants was compiled via organizational charts supplemented by the LinkedIn platform to further identify key individuals. Subsequently, emails were sent to the identified respondents, accompanied by an introductory letter that outlined the research objectives and assured the confidentiality of the responses. The questionnaire, hosted on Google Forms, was then distributed to those who consented to participate. Of the 50 responses received, five were discarded because of missing or incomplete data. As a result, 45 fully completed questionnaires were retained for analysis. Table 1 provides a summary of the sample characteristics and the types of institutions that participated in the study. Notably, all categories of financial institutions were included in the survey, with conventional banks accounting for the largest share at 37.78%, followed by consumer credit companies at 26.67%. Tools and measures To examine the causal relationships between the latent variables in our model, we employed the structural equation modeling (SEM) method, which is based on two main approaches: LISREL and PLS. The choice between these methods depends primarily on the characteristics of the data, such as sample size and the nature of the constructs (Öncel et al., 2023; Næs et al., 2021; Tenenhaus et al., 2004). While other factors, such as the nature of reflective and formative constructs, are also considered, some scholars argue that the literature highlights the existence of latent variables composed of a set of indicators that may not necessarily be correlated with one another (Balambo & El Baz, 2014; Bollen et al., 2000). In this exploratory study, the PLS approach was selected for its methodological flexibility, which is well-suited for models that integrate both reflective and formative latent variables, requiring differentiated assessments of reliability and validity (Lacroux, 2011). This choice is further justified by the nature of our model, which integrates two theoretical frameworks (Simons, 1995; Reynaud, 2003) that, to the best of our knowledge, have not been empirically tested. Overall performance, the endogenous variable in the model, is conceptualized as a formative construct incorporating both financial and nonfinancial indicators, thus providing a more accurate approach to its multidimensional nature. Indeed, overall performance is a multidimensional concept that takes into account economic, social, and environmental aspects (Reynaud, 2003; Capron & Quairel-Lanoizelée, 2006). According to Balambo and El Baz (2014), the most common example of a formative construct in management sciences is overall performance, which is composed of several indicators contributing to its measurement without assuming correlations among them. To operationalize this, we refer to the decomposition of overall performance proposed by Reynaud (2003). First, economic and financial performance was calculated on the basis of net banking income (NBI) and return on assets (ROA) (Moon et al., 2014). Second, social and environmental performance was assessed via indicators proposed by Reynaud, such as the equality of treatment, working conditions, human rights compliance, resource preservation, pollution reduction, and product safety. However, we deemed it appropriate to calculate a composite index in the form of scores for each performance dimension. The CSR strategy variable (CSRS), as a mediating variable, was operationalized on the basis of indicators outlined by the Confederation General of Enterprises (CGEM) charter guidelines, which are aligned with the ISO 26000 international standards. Finally, the operationalization of Simons control levers (exogenous variables) – Belief Systems (SC), Boundary Systems (SF), Diagnostic Control Systems (SCD), and Interactive Control Systems (SCI) – constitutes a major contribution of this research. Specifically, the originality of this work lies in having taken the original measurement items developed within the framework of Simons levers of control and having adapted them to reflect the specific implications and challenges introduced by artificial intelligence. This adaptation process was based on a careful review of validated scales from previous empirical studies (Henri, 2006; Widener, 2007; Tessier & Otley, 2012; Su et al., 2015; Phan et al., 2023), while ensuring that the unique characteristics of AI technologies—such as algorithmic opacity, autonomy in decision-making, and dynamic learning capabilities—were appropriately integrated into the operational definitions of the constructs. Consequently, this methodological choice not only enriches the theoretical framework of management control in the era of AI but also provides a foundation for future empirical investigations in this emerging field. 4. Discussion This study provides compelling empirical evidence on the influence of Simons levers of control in shaping CSR strategy and its subsequent impact on organizational performance. The findings make a significant contribution to the expanding literature on strategic management and CSR governance, particularly within the context of financial institutions operating in emerging economies. The empirical analysis reveals that belief systems and boundary systems exert a significant and positive influence on both CSR strategy and overall performance, highlighting the fundamental role of corporate values and strategic constraints in shaping managerial decisions toward socially responsible business practices. Belief systems facilitate the internalization of CSR principles, whereas boundary systems establish the ethical and structural framework necessary for ensuring compliance with responsible corporate conduct. These findings align with prior research emphasizing the importance of a well-defined strategic vision and strong organizational values in cultivating a robust CSR culture (Gond et al., 2012; Arjaliès & Mundy, 2013). In contrast, diagnostic control systems have a moderate yet statistically significant effect on CSR strategy and overall performance. These mechanisms provide managers with quantitative assessments of CSR initiatives, enabling performance evaluation against predefined objectives (Fitri et al., 2024). However, their effectiveness may be constrained by the complexity and ambiguity of nonfinancial indicators, which poses challenges for decision-making. In this context, AI enhances CSR governance by automating ESG performance assessments, strengthening compliance, and optimizing strategic decision-making through predictive analytics. AI-driven tools foster interactive management by facilitating real-time monitoring, collaborative decision-making, and enhanced transparency through blockchain technologies. Interestingly, interactive control systems do not appear to have a discernible effect on CSR strategy or organizational performance. This implies that Moroccan financial institutions remain within traditional hierarchical management structures, with limited adoption of interactive and participatory governance models. This finding is consistent with the view that in environments where top-down control dominates, interactive systems remain underutilized, limiting their capacity to drive adaptive and innovative CSR strategies (Essid, 2009; Simons, 1995; Widener, 2007). Additionally, this study underscores the mediating role of CSR strategy in enhancing organizational performance. The results indicate that CSR initiatives account for 38% of the variance in performance, reinforcing their strategic importance in long-term value creation and corporate sustainability. However, the analysis also reveals that financial institutions in Morocco primarily adopt a compliance-based (defensive) CSR approach rather than a proactive differentiation-driven strategy. As noted by Kramer and Porter (2011), organizations that integrate CSR into their core competitive strategy are more likely to achieve sustainable competitive advantages; however, this approach remains underdeveloped in the institutions examined in this study. AI has emerged as a key enabler for financial institutions seeking to integrate CSR with corporate performance, allowing for more proactive and differentiated sustainability strategies. By improving data analysis, anomaly detection, and decision- making efficiency, AI enhances resource allocation and optimizes strategic planning, ultimately fostering profitability and strengthening market competitiveness (Mantouzi et al., 2025). Nevertheless, the implications of AI for sustainability are still insufficiently explored (Zhao & Gómez Fariñas, 2023). While AI offers transformative potential in enhancing sustainability, it also introduces risks such as algorithmic bias, ethical dilemmas, and regulatory challenges (Mantouzi & Said, 2026). Without proper oversight, AI may undermine sustainability by complicating the governance of economic, social, and environmental impacts (Baker-Brunnbauer, 2021). Recent studies highlight that ethical concerns—such as data privacy, transparency, and AI-related biases—significantly affect stakeholder trust and corporate legitimacy (Mantouzi et al., 2025; Al-Swidi et al., 2024; Elliott et al., 2021). Addressing these ethical and regulatory challenges is crucial to ensuring that AI-driven CSR strategies align with sustainable and responsible business practices. 6. Final Considerations This study presents both theoretical and empirical contributions to the domain of CSR governance by employing Simons levers of control framework to analyze the interrelationship between management control systems, CSR strategy, and organizational performance. Conducted within the context of emerging economies, with a particular focus on the Moroccan https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mouatassim et al. (2026) 12 financial sector, this research advances the literature on strategic management and management control by clarifying the pathways through which CSR initiatives drive corporate performance. The results underscore the critical influence of belief and boundary systems in fostering CSR-aligned performance, highlighting the role of corporate values and strategic constraints in shaping managerial decision-making. Additionally, diagnostic control systems offer a moderate but significant contribution, particularly through budgetary processes that facilitate the assessment and monitoring of CSR initiatives. However, the negligible impact of interactive control systems suggests that Moroccan financial institutions largely adhere to hierarchical, compliance-focused management models, thereby limiting their ability to develop agile and responsive CSR strategies—an essential factor for long-term competitive advantage. The integration of artificial intelligence into management control systems introduces new dynamics that can transform how Simons control levers function. AI enhances the ability to process and analyze large datasets, offering real-time insights and predictive capabilities that improve the decision-making process. For instance, AI-driven tools can support belief systems by aligning organizational values with data-driven insights, ensuring that CSR strategies reflect corporate ethics. Similarly, boundary systems can benefit from AI through improved monitoring and enforcement of compliance with CSR guidelines and regulations. AI can also refine diagnostic control systems by automating the collection and analysis of performance data, enabling more accurate assessments of CSR outcomes and improving the effectiveness of feedback loops. Finally, AI has the potential to strengthen interactive control systems by fostering continuous interaction between decision-makers and real-time data, facilitating more responsive and flexible management practices. However, despite these opportunities, many organizations, particularly in emerging markets, still face challenges in effectively integrating AI into their control systems. The underutilization of AI tools remains a barrier, highlighting the need for greater awareness and training within organizations to ensure that AI applications are used ethically and in alignment with CSR goals. While this study offers valuable insights, it also acknowledges several limitations that pave the way for future research. First, its sector-specific scope may limit the broader applicability of the findings, necessitating cross-industry comparisons to uncover sectoral differences in CSR implementation. Second, the reliance on perceptual data, although insightful, introduces the possibility of respondent bias. Future research could benefit from a mixed-methods approach, integrating qualitative case studies with quantitative methodologies to increase the validity and reliability of the findings. Third, the study highlights the persistent challenges in measuring CSR performance, underscoring the need for standardized assessment frameworks that improve comparability, inform managerial decision-making, and support corporate sustainability objectives. Furthermore, the underutilization of AI within Moroccan financial institutions emerged as a key limitation. Despite its potential, AI is not yet fully integrated or used strategically in alignment with CSR goals. This underscores the need for greater awareness and training among employees to foster the effective and ethical use of AI tools. Furthermore, this research reinforces the strategic significance of management control systems in enhancing CSR effectiveness and driving organizational performance. As CSR continues to gain prominence as a fundamental pillar of corporate strategy, future studies should explore how AI-driven enhancements to Simons control levers can facilitate CSR governance, enabling more dynamic, responsive, and ethical approaches to corporate sustainability and long-term value creation, particularly within emerging market economies. JSON: Name: ai_mcs_csr_performance Title: PLS-SEM evaluation of AI-augmented management control levers on CSR implementation and overall performance in financial institutions Short Hypothesis: Integrating AI capabilities into belief, boundary, and diagnostic management control systems causally increases CSR implementation effectiveness, which in turn leads to higher overall organizational performance compared to equivalent non-AI-enhanced control systems. Related Work: Existing work operationalizes Simons' levers-of-control (belief, boundary, diagnostic, interactive) to explain strategy implementation and links CSR adoption to multidimensional performance constructs. Prior empirical studies commonly use survey-based measures, exploratory SEM (often PLS-SEM), and archival CSR/ESG disclosures to test associations between MCS configurations and performance. Limitations in the current literature include: (1) predominant focus on external CSR disclosure metrics rather than internal implementation processes and mediating mechanisms; (2) heavy reliance on perceptual cross-sectional surveys with small or sector-limited samples, reducing statistical power and external validity; (3) limited integration of technology adoption—particularly AI—into operational definitions of control levers, producing coarse treatment of automation and analytics capabilities; (4) weak causal identification due to cross-sectional designs and potential endogeneity between MCS and performance; (5) inconsistent treatment of interactive controls and mixed findings about their effect. These gaps leave unresolved whether and which AI-enabled control enhancements produce measurable, mediated improvements in CSR implementation and overall performance. Abstract: This research pipeline tests whether embedding artificial intelligence capabilities into management control levers (belief, boundary, diagnostic, interactive) improves Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) implementation and overall organizational performance in financial institutions. We operationalize AI-enhanced levers as augmentations to traditional MCS indicators (algorithmic monitoring, predictive analytics, automated compliance, AI-supported communication) and model causal paths from AI-augmented levers to CSR implementation and from CSR implementation to a formative overall-performance construct (economic, social, environmental). The primary method is Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with mediation testing and multi-group analyses by institution type and AI adoption level. The main contribution is an empirically testable pipeline that isolates the effect of AI augmentation on internal CSR processes and on downstream performance while comparing AI-augmented and non-augmented models. Expected outcomes are quantified path estimates, explained variance in CSR and performance, and identification of which AI-augmented levers produce the largest mediated performance gains. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Primary survey of managers/CSR officers from financial institutions (target n>=200) measuring MCS levers, AI-augmentation items (binary and continuous adoption metrics), CSR implementation indicators, and control variables (firm size, ownership, market, ROA); (B) Archival firm-level financials and third-party ESG scores for the same institutions over 3 years. Baselines: (1) PLS-SEM model with traditional MCS levers (no AI augmentation); (2) PLS-SEM model with AI-augmentation treated as a separate exogenous predictor; (3) CB-SEM (ML) robustness model. Models to estimate: full mediated model (AI-augmented levers -> CSR implementation -> overall performance), direct-only model (AI-augmented levers -> performance), and alternative ordering (performance -> CSR). Evaluation metrics: measurement model: outer loadings, Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, AVE, HTMT; structural model: path coefficients, t-statistics (bootstrap), p-values, R2, adjusted R2, f2 effect sizes, Q2 predictive relevance, SRMR global fit. Statistical tests: bootstrap resampling = 5000, two-tailed alpha=0.05; VIF for collinearity <5. Comparisons/Ablations: (A) Ablation 1: remove AI augmentation indicators from each lever individually to measure delta R2 and delta path coefficients; (B) Ablation 2: drop interactive control construct to test sensitivity; (C) Multi-group analysis: high-AI adopters vs low/no-AI adopters; (D) Temporal robustness: use lagged archival ESG/financials to test directionality. Additional analyses: endogeneity checks using instrumental-variable PLS or two-stage least squares where feasible (instruments: regulatory exposure, national AI policy adoption index); sensitivity analysis across institution types (bank, microfinance, leasing). Reporting: report standardized path coefficients, bias-corrected bootstrap CIs, model fit indices, and subgroup-specific estimates. Risk Factors and Limitations: Small-sample risk: inability to reach target sample size reduces statistical power and precision of path estimates. Common-method bias: reliance on manager self-reports can inflate relationships between constructs. Endogeneity and reverse causality: CSR implementation and performance may be jointly determined, limiting causal interpretation from cross-sectional data. Measurement error: operationalizing 'AI augmentation' is complex and may conflate varying maturity levels, leading to misclassification. Construct multicollinearity: high correlations among levers or AI indicators can bias coefficient estimates. External validity: findings from Moroccan financial institutions may not generalize to other sectors or jurisdictions with different regulatory, cultural, or technological contexts. Data availability/privacy: access to firm-level archival ESG and financial time series may be restricted. Computational/scalability limits: integrating large-scale AI-usage logs or high-frequency ESG telemetry can require significant storage and processing resources beyond typical survey analysis setups. Ethical/legal constraints: collecting AI usage metrics and internal monitoring data may raise privacy and compliance issues that limit data scope.
